title: The degree-g-minus-one Picard torsor and its determinant theta divisor
statement:
Let $S$ be a locally Noetherian scheme [def-pc-scheme, pqf-def-locnoeth], $g\geq2$, and $f:C\to S$ a smooth stable unpointed genus-$g$ family [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids]. Assume $J=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/S}$ is represented by an algebraic space [sk-def-picard-pic, def-trf-algebraic-space]. Let $P=\operatorname{Pic}^{g-1}_{C/S}$ be the sub-fppf sheaf of line-module classes of fibrewise degree $g-1$, where the degree on a smooth proper geometric curve is $\chi(L)-\chi(\mathcal O)$. Then $P$ is represented by an algebraic space and tensor product makes it a $J$-torsor: the action map gives $J\times_SP\simeq P\times_SP$, and $P$ has sections etale locally on $S$. There is an etale covering family $S_i\to S$ of locally Noetherian schemes on which $C_{S_i}$ has a section $p_i$; the maps
$$\beta_{p_i}:J_{S_i}\xrightarrow{\sim}P_{S_i},\qquad [M]\longmapsto[M\otimes\mathcal O_C((g-1)p_i)]$$
are torsor trivializations.

There is a canonical effective Cartier divisor $\Theta_{C/S}$ on $P$ (on every etale scheme chart of $P$ a closed subscheme locally cut out by one non-zero-divisor), flat over $S$ in the chartwise sense of [def-sfb-space-morphism-properties], with associated invertible module $\mathcal T=\mathcal O_P(\Theta_{C/S})$ [def-pc-divisor-line-bundle, def-sc-invertible-module]. On a scheme chart $V\to P$ carrying a representing invertible module $\mathcal U$ on $C_V$, the complex $Rf_{V,*}\mathcal U$ is locally represented in degrees $0,1$ by a map $d:E^0\to E^1$ of finite locally free modules of the same rank [def-amb-finite-locally-free-module]. Here $Rf_{V,*}$ means the complex obtained by applying $f_{V,*}$ to an injective resolution, considered in the derived category [def-pc-derived-category]. The pullback of the pair $(\mathcal T,s_\Theta)$ is canonically the pair
$$(\det E^1\otimes(\det E^0)^{-1},\det d),$$
where $\det E$ is the highest exterior power [def-sc-sheaf-exterior-power] and $s_\Theta$ is the section cutting out $\Theta_{C/S}$. These pairs are independent of the representative $\mathcal U$ and of the displayed complex. For every geometric point $\operatorname{Spec}K\to S$, the divisor $(\Theta_{C/S})_K$ is the scheme-theoretic image of the Abel morphism from the scheme of effective divisors of degree $g-1$ on $C_K$ [thm-pc-hilb-curves], sending $D$ to $[\mathcal O_{C_K}(D)]$ in $P_K$.

Formation of $P$, its action, the maps $\beta_p$, and the pair $(\mathcal T,s_\Theta)$ commutes with arbitrary base change between locally Noetherian schemes and with isomorphisms of the curve families. For an isomorphism $u:C\xrightarrow{\sim}D$, the induced map $b=(u^{-1})^*:P_C\to P_D$ pulls the pair for $D$ back to the pair for $C$. All these comparisons satisfy identity and composition. No line module on $J$ without a choice of local torsor section is asserted.

proof.text: The family is flat and finitely presented, with nonempty smooth geometrically connected fibres of dimension one, by the stable-family hypothesis; it is proper because it is projective in the projective-bundle sense. Apply universal structure-sheaf pushforward to get $\mathcal O_T\simeq(f_T)_*\mathcal O_{C_T}$ for every $T$. Smoothness and nonempty fibres make $C\to S$ a smooth surjection, so choose an etale cover $S_i\to S$ with sections $p_i$. The $S_i$ are locally Noetherian by local finite type over $S$. Each $p_i$ is an effective Cartier divisor because the curve is separated and smooth of relative dimension one. Its geometric fibre is one rational point, so $\mathcal O((g-1)p_i)$ has degree $g-1$.

proof.text: The full Picard fppf sheaf is a smooth algebraic space by the curve-Picard theorem, using Step 1's universal structure-sheaf condition. Its degree-$r$ subfunctor is open: on $S_i$, every class on a parameter scheme $T$ has a normalized line representative, by rigidification; the locus where $\chi(L_t)-\chi(\mathcal O_{C_t})=r$ is open and closed by Euler local constancy. These loci agree on overlaps since Euler degree is invariant under field extension and base twists. Thus they glue to the required open subscheme of every test scheme $T$; the definition of open subspace makes the subfunctor an algebraic space. In particular $P$ is represented and is smooth over $S$. Here $J=\operatorname{Pic}^0_{C/S}$ is the degree-zero Picard sheaf, in the convention of the statement.

proof.text: Tensor degree is additive on each geometric curve, so tensoring defines $J\times_SP\to P$. For any test scheme the map $(M,L)\mapsto(M\otimes L,L)$ has inverse $(L_1,L_2)\mapsto(L_1\otimes L_2^{-1},L_2)$; both formulas are formulas for Picard sheaf sections, and their composites cancel the dual factors. Thus it is an isomorphism of sheaves and hence of representing spaces. On $S_i$, tensoring by $A_i=\mathcal O((g-1)p_i)$ has inverse tensoring by $A_i^{-1}$ and gives $\beta_{p_i}:J_{S_i}\simeq P_{S_i}$. The class of $A_i$ is a local section of $P$, proving the torsor assertion.

source.place: Tag 0AYX (lemma-degree-tensor-product); Milne III Section 8, degree components of the relative Picard functor.

proof.text: Choose etale scheme charts of $P$ lying over the $S_i$. On each such chart $V$ rigidification along $p_i$ supplies an actual line module $U$ on $C_V$ representing its classifying map. Since $f_V$ is proper, hence quasi-compact and quasi-separated, the etale--Zariski equivalence on $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}$ intertwines the Zariski complex $K=Rf_{V,*}U$ with $R\epsilon_{V,*}Rf_{V,\mathrm{et},*}U$. By perfect coherent base change, $K$ is therefore perfect and its derived pullback is the cohomology complex for every base change. On a geometric fibre it has cohomology only in degrees $0,1$, by the coherent curve vanishing, and its Euler characteristic is $(g-1)+(1-g)=0$, by Riemann--Roch and the definition of degree. On an affine chart, the residue-field criterion puts this perfect object in Tor degrees $[0,1]$. Apply the two-term Tor-window equivalence to $K[1]$ in degrees $[-1,0]$ and reindex back to obtain $E^0\xrightarrow d E^1$ (rescaling one term removes the shift sign). The equality of Euler characteristics forces the ranks of $E^0,E^1$ to agree on each component. Only the fibrewise degree $g-1$ of $U$ was used, so the same holds for any representing module on any scheme chart of $P$.

source.place: Tag 0CTM; more-algebra.tex Tag 068V and lemma-perfect; perfect.tex Tag 0FJX. The [0,1] to [-1,0] reindexing retains the same differential for the displayed determinant formula.

proof.text: Apply the canonical-section lemma to $K$ to obtain $(D(K),\delta_K)$ on $V$ with the displayed exterior-power formula. This immediately removes dependence on a chosen two-term complex, including after adding an acyclic identity complex. If $U'=U\otimes f_V^*N$, the perfect projection formula identifies $Rf_{V,*}U'$ with $K\otimes N$; rank-zero twist cancellation identifies its pair with the old pair. Any two representatives of the same class differ in this way: normalize both along $p_i$ and use rigidification's uniqueness. The choice of an isomorphism between representatives is immaterial, since its ambiguity is a scalar from $V$ by Step 1, and scalars act trivially on the determinant pair. This argument applies also on overlaps where the two chosen curve sections differ: normalize both representatives using either one section on that overlap.

On each double overlap $V_i\times_PV_j$ the pulled-back complexes are the direct images of the pulled-back representatives, by perfect coherent base change along the flat chart maps; use Step 5's comparison there. On a triple overlap, composing the representative isomorphisms tensors their base lines; cancellation for the product twist and functoriality for derived isomorphisms give the same comparison as going directly. Any residual scalar acts trivially. Thus the lines have a genuine etale descent datum and the sections agree under it. Line-module descent gives a line module $\mathcal T$ on $P$; its fully faithful assertion, applied to maps $\mathcal O\to\mathcal T$, glues the sections to $s_\Theta$. Set $\Theta=Z(s_\Theta)$. This is a real zero-scheme construction and on each chart it is locally the principal ideal $(\det d)$.

proof.text: Fix an algebraically closed geometric field $k$ over $S$, and choose $p\in C(k)$. The geometric curve is smooth connected, hence integral: its regular local rings are domains, so distinct irreducible components cannot meet, and connectedness leaves one component. Its degree-zero Picard space is the Jacobian by representability and uniqueness of representing objects. Translate $P_k$ to that Jacobian by $L\mapsto L(-(g-1)p)$. The Abel-image theorem gives an integral effective Cartier divisor $W_{g-1}$, of dimension $g-1$, as the scheme-theoretic image. By the determinant-section lemma, the support of the determinant zero scheme is exactly the locus with $H^0(C,L)\ne0$, since $\chi(L)=0$. A nonzero section of a line on an integral curve cuts out an effective Cartier divisor with $L\simeq\mathcal O(D)$; the degree formula makes its degree $g-1$. Conversely the canonical section of $\mathcal O(D)$ is nonzero. Thus this support is precisely $W_{g-1}$, which is a proper closed subset of the integral $g$-dimensional Jacobian. The determinant section is therefore nonzero and its zero scheme is an effective Cartier divisor.

source.place: III Sections 1, 5--6, especially Theorem 5.1(a), pp.101--102; determinant support: Stacks Section 0FJI. This proves support and Cartierness, not yet scheme equality.

proof.text: Choose an effective divisor $D$ of degree $g-1$ with $h^0(\mathcal O(D))=1$ using the small-degree-divisor lemma, and put $L=\mathcal O(D)$. Riemann--Roch gives $h^1(L)=1$. Choose nonzero $s\in H^0(L)$ and $t\in H^0(\omega_C\otimes L^{-1})$ by Serre duality. Their product is a nonzero canonical differential, since both are nonzero at the generic point of the integral curve. The perfect Serre pairing between $H^1(\mathcal O_C)$ and $H^0(\omega_C)$ supplies $v$ with $\langle v,st\rangle\ne0$. The split-thickening Picard cocycle lemma realizes $v$ as a tangent direction at $L$ in $P_k$. By the first-order-obstruction lemma the induced map $H^0(L)\to H^1(L)$ is nonzero.

proof.text: At $L$ the equal-rank matrix $d_0$ has one-dimensional kernel and cokernel. In a local trivialization an $(r-1)$-minor is a unit. Elementary row and column operations using that minor reduce $d$ to an identity block and one scalar $a$ in the maximal ideal; they change its determinant by a unit. Along Step 8's dual-number direction $\operatorname{Spec}A\to P_k$, perfect coherent base change makes the pulled-back two-term free complex a model of $R\Gamma(C_A,L_A)$; the coefficient of $\epsilon$ in $a$ is the nonzero kernel-to-cokernel obstruction, by the model comparison of the first-order lemma. Consequently the local equation $\det d$ is not in the square of the maximal ideal at $L$. For $r=1$ this is the same argument with an empty identity block. This computes multiplicity at a specified point without assuming any generic smoothness of the Abel map.

source.place: Section 0FJI, determinant of the differential; the Schur-complement computation after choosing a unit minor is ordinary matrix elimination.

proof.text: The geometric Jacobian is smooth, so its local rings are regular, hence unique factorization domains. Let $h$ be a local prime equation for the integral Cartier divisor $W_{g-1}$. Since Step 7 gives equality of supports, the local determinant equation has no prime factor except $h$, and so is $u h^n$ with $u$ a unit and $n\ge1$. At Step 8's point, $n>1$ would put this equation in the square of the maximal ideal, contradicting Step 9. Therefore its order at the generic point of $W_{g-1}$ is one. At every other point of $W_{g-1}$ the exponent is the same generic order (localizing at $(h)$ gives the generic DVR), so $n=1$ everywhere. The determinant ideal and the ideal of $W_{g-1}$ consequently agree at every stalk. This proves equality with the scheme-theoretic Abel image, including its multiplicity and not just its set of points.

proof.text: For an etale scheme chart $V\to P$, the map $V\to S$ is flat and locally finitely presented, since $P\to S$ is smooth (Step 2). The subscheme $Z(s_\Theta)|_V$ is locally principal. Steps 7--10 show that its every geometric fibre is an effective Cartier divisor. This also holds over the residue fields themselves: after a faithfully flat algebraic field extension, injectivity of multiplication by a local equation reflects back, since tensor with a field extension is faithful. Apply the local fibre-Cartier criterion at each point. It gives that $\Theta|_V$ is effective Cartier and flat over $S$. These are exactly the asserted chartwise properties on $P$. A regular line section gives its divisor line canonically: in a local frame $e$ with $s=a e$, the ideal is $(a)$ and the identification $\mathcal I^{-1}\simeq\mathcal T$ sends the functional $a\mapsto1$ to $e$. These identifications agree on changes of frame, and their distinguished section is $s_\Theta$. Thus $\mathcal T\simeq\mathcal O_P(\Theta)$.

source.place: Tag 062Y (lemma-fibre-Cartier), part (3); the divisor-line identification is the local dual-ideal formula.

proof.text: Base change restricts the Picard sheaf and preserves fibre degrees, so it preserves $P$, $J$, the tensor action and the tensor formulas for $\beta_p$. Pulling a section divisor through a base change preserves it and its line module; hence the reference $\mathcal O((g-1)p)$ also pulls back. On each representing chart, perfect coherent base change identifies the new direct-image complex with $Lh^*K$. The canonical-section lemma identifies the resulting determinant pair with the pulled-back pair, compatibly with changing representatives. By the fully faithful descent of maps of lines these local comparisons give the global comparison of $(\mathcal T,s_\Theta)$, and hence of its zero divisor, for arbitrary locally Noetherian base change. In particular the fibre comparisons used in Steps 7--10 are comparisons of the constructed pair.

For a family isomorphism $u:C\simeq D$, the map $b=(u^{-1})^*:P_C\to P_D$ sends a representing line $U$ to $(u^{-1})^*U$; pulling it back along $u$ recovers $U$. Since $u$ is an isomorphism, its inverse-image and direct-image functors are inverse exact equivalences on module sheaves. Applying them to an injective resolution gives the canonical identification of the two derived direct images, compatible with identity and composition. The determinant functor and section transport this identification to $b^*(\mathcal T_D,s_D)\simeq(\mathcal T_C,s_C)$. The same tensor identities give compatibility for the action and for $\beta_p$ with $p$ transported to $u(p)$. For two base changes, two family isomorphisms, or their combination, the comparisons on lines are the functorial ones for pulled-back complexes and rank-zero twists; their identity and composition laws follow from the corresponding laws of the canonical-section lemma and perfect base change. Fully faithful line descent checks the same equations globally. No point or degree-$g-1$ class is selected globally in this construction.
